(a) Write one statistical question about how Class 7 students come to school. (b) Explain why 'What time did Isha reach school today?' is not one.
questions.a: (a) For example: How long do Class 7 students take to reach school? The answers vary from child to child. (b) It asks about one person on one day, so there is a single answer and no data to collect or compare.

Part (b): says it has one answer so no data needs collecting

questions.a: (a) She took 10 wickets in 5 matches, that is 2 wickets per match on average. (b) How many wickets does she usually take in a match?
s: Part (a): a statement with a number from the data (total 10 or average 2)
Part (b): a question that expects varied answers and needs this data

questions.q: (a) Are these statistical questions? (i) What fraction of Grade 7 students like walking up a hill? (ii) How many legs does a spider have? (b) Give the reason for your answer to (ii).

Describes a statistical statement and gives a valid example

questions.a: Yes. The question asks about a whole group, and the times are expected to vary from child to child. It can only be answered by collecting many times, whereas Kavya's single reading is one value, not the answer.
s: Gives the verdict that Rafi is right
Reason: the answers are expected to vary across students
Reason: it needs data from many students, not one reading

questions.q: Decide which are statistical questions and give a reason for each. (i) How much pocket money do Class 7 students in Hyderabad get weekly? (ii) How many chapters does the Part II textbook have? (iii) Typically, is a cinema ticket costlier in Pune or Nagpur?
questions.a: (i) Yes, amounts differ so data is needed. (ii) No, it has one fixed answer found by counting the contents page. (iii) Yes, prices vary over time and shows, so we need to look at data.
s: (i) identified as statistical with a reason

questions.q: At the Class 7 sports day, Ms Verma wants to know how long her students take to run 100 m. Five students took 16, 18, 15, 17 and 16 seconds. (a) Write a statistical question for her. (b) Find the total and the average time. (c) Write a statistical statement. (d) Why must she collect more than one student's time?
questions.a: (a) How long do Class 7 students take to run 100 m? (b) total 16+18+15+17+16 = 82 s, average 82/5 = 16.4 s. (c) The students took about 16.4 seconds on average. (d) One time is one answer; times vary, so many values are needed to describe the group.
s: Part (c): a statement using the numbers
Part (d): says answers vary so many values are needed

questions.q: Four students make claims. Neha: 'On average our class is taller than yours.' Imran: 'The school bell rang at 8 a.m. today.' Joseph: 'Most Class 7 students cycle to school.' Sakshi: 'What is the date of the school fair?' (a) Which two claims are statistical statements? (b) Which one is a question, and is it a statistical question? (c) Rewrite Neha's claim as a statistical statement that uses two numbers. (d) Give a statistical question that Joseph's claim could answer.
questions.a: (a) Neha's (it summarises and compares groups) and Joseph's (a proportion, most). Imran's is a single fact for one moment, not a summary of data. (b) Sakshi's; not statistical, it has one fixed answer. (c) For example: The mean height of our class is 146 cm and of yours is 143 cm. (d) How do Class 7 students come to school?
s: Part (a): picks Neha and Joseph with a reason
Part (b): picks Sakshi and says it is not statistical
Part (c): a statement with two numbers comparing the classes
Part (d): a statistical question on travel to school

questions.q: Mrs Rao, the school librarian, noted the books issued on six school days: Monday 12, Tuesday 18, Wednesday 9, Thursday 15, Friday 21, Saturday 15. Her rule is to restock when more than 100 books are issued in a week. (a) Is 'How many books does the library issue on a typical day?' a statistical question? Why? (b) How many books were issued in the six days? (c) Write one statistical statement using the average per day. (d) Should she restock now, or keep recording for more weeks? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Yes, daily numbers vary and need data. (b) 90 books. (c) On average 15 books were issued per day (90 / 6). (d) 90 is below 100, so by her rule she should not restock yet; but it is close and the days range from 9 to 21, and one week is a small sample, so she should keep recording for more weeks before deciding. Restocking early is also defensible if she values never running short.
s: Part (a): yes because daily numbers vary and need data
Part (c): statement with average 15 per day
Part (d): a justified decision using the rule 100 and the size of the sample

questions.q: Sneha tells her mother, 'I take about 15 minutes to cycle from school to home.' To check, she timed herself on five days and got 14, 18, 15, 22 and 16 minutes. Her mother wants to start the pressure cooker just before she arrives. (a) Write a statistical question that Sneha's timings help to answer. (b) Find the total time and the mean time. (c) Does the data support 'about 15 minutes'? (d) What should Sneha tell her mother about her arrival time, so that the lunch is neither cold nor wasted?
questions.a: (a) How long does Sneha usually take to cycle home? (b) total 85 minutes, mean 17 minutes. (c) Not really: the mean is 17; three of the five days were 16 minutes or more, and one was 22. (d) Say she usually takes about 17 minutes and may take up to about 22; start the cooker after she leaves school.
s: Part (a): a statistical question about her usual time
Part (c): compares 15 with 17 and the spread
Part (d): a justified recommendation using mean and the range

The number of flowers on a hibiscus plant on six days was 4, 9, 2, 7, 3 and 5. (a) Find the mean number of flowers per day. (b) On the seventh day 11 flowers bloom. Find the new mean, correct to two decimal places.
questions.a: (a) 30 / 6 = 5 flowers per day. (b) (30 + 11) / 7 = 41 / 7 = 5.86 flowers per day.
s: Part (b): uses total 41 and 7 days to get 5.86

questions.q: A student's mean mark in 7 unit tests is 14. (a) Find the total of her 7 marks. (b) She scores 22 in the eighth test. What is her mean for 8 tests?
s: Part (a): total = mean x number of tests = 98
Part (b): adds 22 to get 120 and divides by 8 to get 15

questions.q: Anil took 16, 17, 15, 18 and 16 seconds and Bela took 17, 15, 16, 15 and 16 seconds in five 100 m trial runs. (a) Find each runner's mean time. (b) Who is quicker on average and by how many seconds?
questions.a: (a) Anil: 82 / 5 = 16.4 s. Bela: 79 / 5 = 15.8 s. (b) Bela is quicker by 0.6 s on average.
s: Part (b): names Bela and the difference 0.6 s

questions.q: Five children pool 7, 3, 9, 5 and 11 marbles and share them equally. How many does each get? Explain how this is linked to the mean.
questions.a: Total 35, each gets 35 / 5 = 7 marbles. The mean is the equal share: the number each would have if all values were levelled out.
s: Links the equal share to the mean as a levelled-out value

questions.q: What does the old Indian name samamiti tell us about how ancient scholars saw the arithmetic mean? Name one scholar who used it.
questions.a: They saw the mean as an equal or common value that represents a collection (sama means equal, miti means measure). Bhaskaracharya (also Ganesha) used the term samamiti.
s: Explains that it is the equalising or common value

questions.q: Dhruv says, 'Club A scored 215 runs in 5 matches and Club B scored 192 runs in 4 matches. A has the bigger total so A batted better.' Do you agree? Support your answer with numbers.
questions.a: No. The groups are different sizes, so totals mislead. Club A's mean is 215 / 5 = 43 runs a match and Club B's is 192 / 4 = 48, so B did better per match.
s: Verdict that Dhruv is wrong because the number of matches differs

questions.q: Show that the mean of 12, 15, 18 and 21 cannot be 25 or 10.
questions.a: The mean levels the values out, so it lies between the smallest and the largest value: 12 and 21. The actual mean is 66 / 4 = 16.5. 25 is above 21 and 10 is below 12, so neither is possible.
s: States that the mean lies between smallest and largest

questions.q: A railway booking counter sold 3150, 3480, 3610, 3200, 3920 and 3640 tickets in six consecutive weeks. (a) Find the mean number of tickets per week. (b) In how many of the six weeks were the sales above the mean?
questions.a: (a) Total 21000, mean 21000 / 6 = 3500. (b) 3610, 3920 and 3640 are above 3500, so 3 weeks.

questions.q: The mean marks of a student in 5 tests is 72. (a) Find the total of her 5 marks. (b) Four of the marks are 68, 75, 80 and 65. Find the fifth. (c) What mark in a sixth test (out of 100) makes her mean for 6 tests 75? (d) Can she reach a mean of 80 over 6 tests? Explain.
questions.a: (a) 72 x 5 = 360. (b) 360 - (68 + 75 + 80 + 65) = 360 - 288 = 72. (c) 75 x 6 = 450, so 450 - 360 = 90. (d) A mean of 80 needs a total of 480, so the sixth mark would be 120, more than 100. Not possible.
s: Part (c): sixth mark 90 with the method total = mean x number
Part (d): needs 120 which exceeds 100, so impossible

questions.q: Two groups of children share paper cranes equally within the group. Group P (4 children) folded 9, 12, 7 and 8 cranes. Group Q (6 children) folded 6, 8, 5, 9, 7 and 5 cranes. (a) Find the total of each group. (b) Find each child's equal share in each group. (c) Which group has the greater total and which the greater share? (d) Which measure should be used to say which group did better, and why?
questions.a: (a) P: 36, Q: 40. (b) P: 36 / 4 = 9, Q: 40 / 6 = 6.67 (about 6.7). (c) Q has the greater total, P the greater share. (d) The mean, because the groups differ in size and the mean is the fair share per child.
s: Part (d): chooses the mean with a reason about unequal group sizes

questions.q: Classes 7A and 7B ran a savings drive for a flood-relief fund. The six students of the 7A savings club saved ₹240, 180, 300, 120, 260 and 100. The eight students of the 7B club saved ₹150, 200, 170, 220, 90, 280, 160 and 250. The principal can give a trophy for either the larger collection or the larger saving per student. (a) Find the total saved by each club. (b) Find each club's mean saving per student. (c) What does the mean tell us here in terms of equal shares? (d) The principal must pick one measure for the trophy. Which would you advise, and what is the case for the other measure?
questions.a: (a) 7A: 1200, 7B: 1520. (b) 7A: 200, 7B: 190. (c) If every student had saved the same amount, each of 7A would have saved 200 and each of 7B 190. (d) Per-student mean favours 7A and is fair when clubs differ in size; the total favours 7B because it has more members. Either is defensible but the mean is fairer to a smaller club.
s: Part (c): explains the mean as an equal share
Part (d): a justified choice that weighs both measures

questions.q: A farmer in Wayanad records rainfall in mm on five days: 12, 0, 25, 8 and 15. A day with no rain is recorded as 0. He irrigates his pepper plants only if the mean daily rainfall of the week so far is below 14 mm. (a) Find the mean rainfall for the five days. (b) Should the zero be counted as a day? Explain. (c) On day six the rain gauge shows 30 mm. Find the new mean. (d) Based on (a) and (c), would he have irrigated on day five, and does the day six reading change his decision?
questions.a: (a) 60 / 5 = 12 mm. (b) Yes: a 0 means it was measured and no rain fell, so the day counts. (c) (60 + 30) / 6 = 15 mm. (d) On day five the mean 12 is below 14, so he irrigates; with 15 on day six it is above 14, so he need not irrigate any more.
s: Part (b): counts the zero with a reason
Part (d): decides using both means against 14

questions.q: Team A scored 14, 9, 11, 16, 10 and 12 points in six games and Team B scored 13, 13, 12, 14 and 13 points in five games. (a) Find each team's total. (b) Explain why the totals alone cannot say which team scored better per game.

s: Part (b): says the numbers of games differ so means are needed

questions.q: (a) What does a dot plot lose that the original table of monthly prices has? (b) Name one thing a dot plot makes easy to see.
questions.a: (a) The month-wise sequence of the values; from a dot plot we cannot tell January's price. (b) The spread or the clusters of the data, or the highest and lowest values.
s: Part (a): the original order is lost

questions.q: Besides the mean, name four numbers that the chapter uses to describe and compare two sets of data.

questions.q: The price of a notebook in town X over five months was ₹22, 25, 24, 30 and 22. (a) Find the range. (b) If the price in town Y has range 3 over the same months, which town's prices are steadier?
questions.a: (a) 30 - 22 = 8. (b) Town Y, because a smaller range shows less variation.
s: Part (b): town Y with a reason about smaller range

questions.q: In five practice matches Mira scored 40, 42, 41, 43 and 44 and Tej scored 20, 60, 25, 70 and 30. Sana says, 'The ranges are 4 and 50, so Mira's scores are steadier. The totals, 210 and 205, are almost equal, so I cannot say Mira scored more.' Do you agree?
questions.a: Yes. Mira's range is 44 - 40 = 4 and Tej's is 70 - 20 = 50, so Mira's scores vary much less. The totals 210 and 205 differ by only 5 over the same five matches, so the total gives no clear winner. Both parts of her claim follow from the data.
s: Checks the ranges 4 and 50 to support 'steadier'
Uses totals 210 and 205 to support 'cannot say who scored more'

questions.q: A club says: 'Our five players' scores have a range of 4, but the highest score was 50 and the lowest was 40.' Show that this cannot be true.
questions.a: Range = maximum - minimum = 50 - 40 = 10, not 4. So the claim contradicts itself.
s: Concludes the stated range 4 is impossible

questions.q: A shopkeeper's daily sales (₹ thousand) in Pune for six days are 18, 22, 15, 30, 25 and 20. (a) Find the total sales. (b) Find the range. (c) If days are grouped as 15-20, 21-25 and 26-30, which group holds the most days?
questions.a: (a) 130. (b) 30 - 15 = 15. (c) 15-20 holds 18, 15 and 20 (three days), 21-25 holds 22 and 25 (two days) and 26-30 holds only 30, so 15-20 holds the most.
s: Identifies the 15-20 group with three days

questions.q: The monthly prices of milk (₹ per litre) in two towns for six months are: Town P 44, 46, 45, 52, 47, 46 and Town Q 45, 45, 46, 46, 47, 45. (a) Find the total of each town. (b) Find each range. (c) Find each mean. (d) Which town has the more stable price, and which has the higher average?
questions.a: (a) P: 280, Q: 274. (b) P: 8, Q: 2. (c) P: 46.67, Q: 45.67. (d) Q is more stable (range 2); P has the higher average.

questions.q: Aman compares his and Dia's 50 m dash times (seconds) in five practice runs. Aman: 12, 12, 13, 12, 13. Dia: 10, 11, 10, 11, 18. (a) Find each total. (b) Find each range. (c) Find each mean. (d) The school relay needs a runner whose time can be trusted on race day, but the coach also wants the fastest average. Whom would you pick, and what is the case for the other runner?
questions.a: (a) Aman 62, Dia 60. (b) Aman 1, Dia 8. (c) Aman 12.4, Dia 12. (d) Dia is faster on average (12 against 12.4) but one run of 18 shows he can be far slower; Aman never varies by more than 1 second. For a reliable leg pick Aman; the case for Dia is the lower total and mean, and four of his five runs were quicker than any of Aman's.
s: Part (d): a justified pick weighing mean against range

questions.q: A vegetable seller compared tomato prices (₹ per kg) in Nashik and Indore for eight weeks. Nashik: 18, 22, 25, 40, 38, 20, 24, 19. Indore: 25, 27, 26, 30, 29, 28, 27, 26. (a) Find the total for each town. (b) Find each range. (c) In how many weeks was Indore costlier than Nashik? (d) A trader must pick one town to buy from in a week when he cannot predict the price. Which town do you advise, and why?
questions.a: (a) Nashik 206, Indore 218. (b) 22 and 5. (c) 6 weeks. (d) Nashik is cheaper in total (206 < 218) and Indore costlier in 6 of 8 weeks, but Nashik can spike to 40. A trader who wants safety picks Indore (range 5); one who wants low cost on average picks Nashik.
s: Part (d): a justified choice weighing cost against variation

questions.q: Class 7 of a school in Chennai logged the time (minutes) for its Section A and Section B teams to finish a puzzle relay on five days. Section A: 21, 25, 19, 30, 22. Section B: 24, 23, 25, 22, 24. (a) Find the total time and range for each section. (b) Whose times are more spread out? (c) Section A says 'we were quickest on one day, so we are the better team.'
